questions.passage: For most of the twentieth century, psychologists treated forgetting as a simple failure of storage—memories faded because their traces decayed. On a newer account, much of what we call forgetting is instead a form of active editing: the brain suppresses older associations precisely so that newer, more useful ones can be retrieved without interference. Forgetting, in this light, is less the enemy of memory than one of its instruments.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces an alternative explanation that recasts the phenomenon described in the first sentence, setting up the reappraisal stated in the last.
It provides experimental evidence that confirms the traditional view of forgetting described in the first sentence.
It defines a technical term that the remainder of the passage goes on to dispute.
It raises an objection to the newer account that the final sentence concedes.

questions.passage: Economic historians disagree about why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain rather than in similarly wealthy parts of Asia. One scholar emphasizes cheap coal: Britain's mines sat close to its cities and workshops. Had coal been as costly to move in Britain as it was elsewhere, this argument implies, mechanization would have offered manufacturers little advantage over hand labor.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the underlined claim?
options: In regions where coal lay far from manufacturing centers, the fuel cost of running early steam engines exceeded the wages of the workers those engines would have replaced.
Britain's earliest factories were built beside fast-flowing rivers and relied on water power rather than on coal.
Several regions of Asia possessed substantially larger coal reserves than Britain did.
British inventors of the period corresponded frequently with engineers on the European continent.

questions.passage: Legal reformers often assume that writing rules in plainer language will make them fairer, since more people will understand them. But a rule can be perfectly clear and still be unjust, and a vague standard—“reasonable care,” say—can protect people precisely because it leaves room for the judgment that a rigid, transparent rule would foreclose. Clarity, the point suggests, is a virtue of legal language, not a substitute for justice in it.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It supplies an example that supports the assumption stated in the first sentence.
It restates the claim of the first sentence using a specific legal illustration.
It complicates the assumption stated in the first sentence, preparing the distinction drawn in the last.
It concedes a weakness in the position that the passage ultimately defends.

questions.passage: Thomas thanked his employer warmly and asked for a day to consider. That evening he sat with the letter open before him and made, on a half-sheet of paper, two neat columns of reasons; and though the column headed For grew steadily the longer, he found, when the candle had burned low, that he had not so much as touched his pen to the paper for an hour, but had been looking instead at the narrow street below, where the lamplighter was going his round as he had gone every night of Thomas's life.
questions.question: Which choice best describes what the text most strongly suggests about Thomas?
options: He is confident that the reasons against the move outweigh those in its favor.
He resents his employer for presenting him with so difficult a choice.
Despite the practical case for accepting the offer, he is held back by an attachment to the familiar life he would have to leave.
He had resolved to decline the promotion even before he drew up his lists.

questions.passage: Popular accounts often credit the gut's bacteria with controlling human moods, citing studies in which transplanting microbes between animals seems to transfer behaviors along with them. But the pathways are tangled and run in both directions: stress alters the microbiome as surely as the microbiome may alter stress, and most findings in mice have not held up cleanly in people. What the research supports is not a chain of command running from bacteria to brain, but a loop in which each continually reshapes the other.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The link between gut bacteria and mood is better understood as a two-way interaction than as one-directional control.
Gut bacteria have been conclusively shown to determine human moods.
Studies conducted in mice can reveal nothing at all about human beings.
Stress is the single most important influence on the composition of the microbiome.

questions.passage: The town had not changed, and that was the strangeness of it. The same striped awnings, the same gulls quarreling over the same jetty; even the bakery still misspelled Fresh on its window in the same blue paint. Marta had prepared herself to find everything smaller, as returning travelers are warned they will. What she had not prepared for was to find it all exactly as large as before, and herself the only thing in it that no longer quite fit.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The town's very unchangedness makes Marta newly aware of how much she herself has changed.
Marta is disappointed to find that her hometown has deteriorated in her absence.
Marta discovers that her memories had greatly exaggerated the size of the town.
The townspeople have failed to recognize Marta since her return from abroad.

questions.passage: The essayist Neil Farhad is known for undercutting his own grand pronouncements a beat after making them, deflating the very authority he has just claimed. A critic illustrating this self-puncturing manner might quote the line in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Farhad's essays most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “I have spent thirty years studying these questions, and I mean to spend thirty more.”
“History, I am convinced, bends inevitably toward justice—or it would, if it could ever be troubled to remember where it had left off.”
“The archives, as any honest scholar will freely admit, are maddeningly incomplete.”
“It is the first duty of the essayist to say plainly what he means.”

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • A study compared the water use of two crops grown in the same climate.
  • Crop M yields 3.0 tons per hectare and uses 900 mm of water per season.
  • Crop N yields 3.0 tons per hectare and uses 500 mm of water per season.
  • Water use efficiency is the yield obtained per unit of water.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in the two crops' water use. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A study compared the water use of two crops grown in the same climate.
Crop N uses 500 mm of water per season and yields 3.0 tons per hectare.
Water use efficiency is defined as the yield obtained per unit of water.
Although Crops M and N produce the same yield (3.0 tons per hectare), Crop M requires 900 mm of water per season—nearly twice the 500 mm that Crop N requires.

questions.passage:

  • The dodo, a flightless pigeon, evolved on an island with no native mammalian predators.
  • Both birds lost the ability to fly.
  • Both declined rapidly once humans introduced mammalian predators.
questions.question: The student wants to make a generalization about the two birds that is supported by the notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both the kakapo and the dodo evolved flightlessness on islands lacking mammalian predators and then declined sharply once such predators arrived.
The dodo was a flightless pigeon, whereas the kakapo is a flightless parrot.
The kakapo evolved on islands that had no native mammalian predators.
Humans have introduced mammalian predators to many islands around the world.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Some scientists study terra preta in the hope of improving modern agriculture.

Some scientists study terra preta in the hope of improving modern agriculture.
Terra preta is an exceptionally fertile dark soil that ancient Amazonian peoples created—rather than nature—by enriching poor tropical soil with charcoal, pottery, and organic waste.
Terra preta is a fertile dark soil that is found in the Amazon.

  • Species G: relative brain size index 4.5; average lifespan 41 years.

A higher index indicates a larger brain relative to body size.
Species G had a larger relative brain size than both Species F and Species H.
The species with the largest relative brain size, G (index 4.5), had the longest average lifespan (41 years), while the species with the smallest, F (index 1.2), had the shortest (8 years).

questions.passage: Museum curators once treated a painting's discolored varnish as damage to be stripped away, restoring the work to what they took to be its original brilliance. Some conservators now argue that such restorations can destroy evidence—layers of dirt and later retouching that record how a work was seen and valued across the centuries. A painting, on this view, is not only an object but a history, and cleaning it may edit that history as much as reveal it.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers technical detail explaining how varnish is physically removed from paintings.
It concedes a drawback of the newer conservation approach that it goes on to reject.
It presents a countervailing view that reframes an established practice, leading to the reconception offered in the final sentence.
It restates the curators' traditional rationale in more forceful terms.

questions.passage: A familiar story holds that a single roadside diner, opened in 1952, invented the fast-food model that later chains merely copied. Business records tell a messier tale: several unconnected restaurants across three states had adopted nearly identical methods—limited menus, assembly-line kitchens, no table service—within the same few years, none aware of the others. What looks in hindsight like a single origin was in fact a solution that the conditions of the era invited many to reach at once.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a business model, lists its defining features, and then predicts its eventual decline.
It recounts a popular origin story, presents evidence that contradicts it, and then offers a different account of how the development arose.
It introduces a historical dispute, weighs the evidence on each side, and then declines to resolve it.
It profiles an influential restaurant and traces the chains that went on to imitate it.

questions.passage: I do not propose, in these pages, to add another name to the long list of candidates for the poem's authorship. My aim is to show why the question, as usually posed, cannot be answered: the very documents that might settle it were, I will argue, produced by people with strong reasons to disguise who wrote what. Until we reckon with that motive, each new attribution merely repeats the error of trusting the record at face value.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To propose a new and better-supported candidate for the poem's authorship.
To argue that the poem's authorship cannot be settled because the relevant records were deliberately misleading.
To survey the leading theories scholars have advanced about the poem's authorship.
To demonstrate that the poem must have been written by more than one author.

questions.passage: A linguist argues that a newly documented language is unrelated to any known family, since its core vocabulary—words for body parts, numbers, and kinship—shows no systematic correspondences with neighboring languages. Such correspondences, she maintains, are the only reliable proof of common descent; their absence here shows that the language stands alone.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the underlined claim?
options: The languages neighboring the newly documented one themselves belong to three different, unrelated families.
The newly documented language has borrowed many words for modern technology from a former colonial language.
Several well-established language families include members whose core vocabularies were almost entirely replaced through prolonged contact, obscuring a common descent that other evidence confirms.
Fewer than five hundred people now speak the newly documented language.

questions.passage: It is tempting to measure a scientific field's health by how much its practitioners agree. But a field can be unanimous because its central questions have been settled or because they have simply been abandoned as unanswerable, and from the outside the two look identical. Consensus, then, tells us less about progress than the confident metric suggests.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It supplies evidence confirming that consensus is a reliable sign of a field's health.
It distinguishes two very different sources of a single phenomenon, undercutting the assumption stated in the first sentence.
It offers an example of a scientific field that has abandoned its central questions.
It concedes a limitation of the argument advanced in the final sentence.

questions.passage: The stranger who complains that a great city is cold has mistaken its nature. A village may love you, for it has leisure and few to love; a city cannot, for it has neither. But what the city withholds in warmth it returns in freedom: nowhere is a person so unobserved, so unpestered by the expectations of others, so free to become whatever he privately intends. The coldness the newcomer laments is only the far side of the liberty he came to find.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The impersonality that newcomers dislike in cities is inseparable from the very freedom that draws them there.
Cities would be far more pleasant to live in if they cultivated the warmth of villages.
People who move to cities soon come to miss the affection of the villages they left behind.
Large cities are, on the whole, colder and less welcoming places than small villages.

questions.passage: A physiologist proposes that the reason certain trees survive wildfires is not that their bark resists heat chemically but that it insulates so well that the living tissue beneath never reaches a lethal temperature, even as the outer surface chars. On this hypothesis, thickness, not chemistry, is what protects the tree.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the physiologist's hypothesis?
options: The charred outer bark of surviving trees was found to contain compounds known to be flame-retardant.
Trees with thinner bark tended to grow in wetter areas that were less prone to fire.
Among trees of the same species, individuals with thicker bark survived fires that killed thinner-barked individuals, regardless of any differences in bark chemistry.
The living tissue of trees of this species is damaged at temperatures above 60°C.

questions.question: The student wants to explain what a keystone species is to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

  • Group 1 (no training) improved by 3 words per minute over the study.
